clue.text: Arboreal garden feature — hardly to scale?

explanation.surface: A tree in the garden that would be almost impossible to climb.
explanation.walkthrough: The second definition reads the tree's name literally: its spiky branches would leave even a monkey baffled about how to climb it.
explanation.definitionFit: The Chile pine is an ornamental garden tree, and its prickly, overlapping leaves supposedly make it a puzzle for any climbing primate.

clue.text: Art master's pet dog

parts.note: MA is a Master of Arts, and the possessive adds S
a pet is a fit of sulking, as in 'in a pet', the same as a tiff

explanation.surface: An artist's favourite dog.
explanation.walkthrough: 'pet' looks like the animal, but it is an old word for a fit of bad temper, a TIFF.
explanation.definitionFit: A mastiff is a large, powerful breed of guard hound.

clue.text: Leading feature is about nothing but a cow-catcher

indicators.note: the first piece goes about, that is around, the zero

parts.note: the nose is the facial feature that leads the way
O is the round figure zero, nothing

explanation.surface: A prominent part of the face reduced to nothing more than a device on a locomotive.
explanation.walkthrough: 'cow-catcher' suggests the grid on the front of a train, but it is a lasso loop that catches cattle; 'but a' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: A running loop on a rope, as in a lasso, is used to catch cattle.

clue.text: An additional hundred rise : for 'dentist ?

parts.note: something extra is additional
C is the Roman numeral for a hundred
a tor is a rocky hill, a rise in the land

explanation.surface: A dentist getting another hundred pounds as a pay rise.
explanation.walkthrough: 'rise' suggests a pay increase but is a hill, TOR, as on Dartmoor. The definition is playful: a dentist is one who extracts teeth.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone who pulls teeth out is, in a whimsical sense, one who extracts.

clue.text: Get ready to leave the deck

definitions.meaning: to put belongings in a case before a trip
a full set of playing cards

explanation.surface: Preparing to go ashore from a ship's deck.
explanation.definitionFit: To fill a suitcase before travelling; also a complete set of playing cards.

clue.text: Not the time when nothing happens though

definitions.text: Not the time when nothing happens though

parts.words: Not the time when nothing happens though
parts.note: the name literally suggests an hour of nothing, yet it is the moment an operation is launched

explanation.surface: A remark that this is anything but a quiet moment.
explanation.walkthrough: The name seems to promise an hour of nothing, but it is the moment set for an attack or launch, when everything starts.
explanation.definitionFit: The planned starting moment of a military operation, when action begins.

clue.text: It is even palindromic

indicators.note: palindromic says the word reads the same in both directions

parts.note: these definition words give the whole answer, and the answer is itself the palindrome: it reads the same from either end

explanation.surface: Something that is even, and spelt the same either way.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition is 'even', meaning flat; 'It is' leads into it.
explanation.definitionFit: Flat and smooth, with no bumps or slopes.

clue.text: Colour of a proper flower

parts.note: prim means prudishly proper
a rose is a flower

explanation.surface: Asking the colour of a respectable bloom.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface suggests a flower, which the answer also is, but here it is the pale yellow colour; 'of a' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: A pale greenish yellow, named after the spring flower.

clue.text: Mistaken that these sweets are sweeter ?

definitions.meaning: the proverb says forbidden fruit tastes sweetest when it is pilfered

explanation.surface: Doubting the claim that some sweets taste better than others.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Mistaken' looks like 'wrong', but split as mis-taken it means taken wrongfully; the second part recalls the proverb 'stolen waters are sweet'.
explanation.definitionFit: Taken without right, that is pilfered; and pilfered treats are proverbially the tastiest.

clue.text: Diversion mark for motorway flier

parts.note: a diversion is an amusement or pastime, a sport
a scar is a mark left on the skin

explanation.surface: A detour sign set up for a speeding driver on the motorway.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Diversion' suggests a road detour, which suits the motorway picture, but here it means a pastime. 'for' is a link word.
explanation.definitionFit: A fast two-seater car built for speed is something that flies along a motorway.

clue.text: Well acquainted, we hear,'with the Russian measure

indicators.note: says the word for 'well acquainted' is to be spoken, giving a word of the same sound

parts.note: to be versed in something is to be well acquainted with it

explanation.surface: Someone claims to know all about an old unit of length used in Russia.
explanation.definitionFit: An old Russian unit of distance, a little over a kilometre.

clue.text: It should ensure a polar explorer keeping a cool head

definitions.text: It should ensure a polar explorer keeping a cool head

parts.words: It should ensure a polar explorer keeping a cool head
parts.note: reads as advice about headgear for an Arctic traveller, but the cool head is the frozen top of the globe itself

explanation.surface: Advice on what a polar explorer should wear to stay calm.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Keeping a cool head' sounds like staying calm; the cryptic reading is a covering of ice on the polar region, a literal cap that is cold.
explanation.definitionFit: A permanent sheet of ice covering a polar region, the 'cap' on top of the Earth.

clue.text: Poetic singer in Berkeley Square

parts.note: points to the popular song 'A Nightingale Sang in Berkeley Square' and asks for the poets' name for that bird

explanation.surface: A poet performing songs in a smart London square.
explanation.walkthrough: Berkeley Square is a square in London's Mayfair, made famous by the 1940 song 'A Nightingale Sang in Berkeley Square'.
explanation.definitionFit: In poetry the nightingale is called by the name of Philomela from Greek myth, who was turned into the bird.

clue.text: Walks on air in a carnival procession

definitions.meaning: drifts weightlessly as if on air; the verb sense
the decorated vehicles carrying displays in a parade; the noun sense

explanation.surface: Someone so happy they feel weightless during a carnival parade.
explanation.definitionFit: The verb means drifts lightly in air or water; the plural noun names decorated lorries in a parade.

clue.text: Brief inspection -as, soon, as finished

parts.note: once can mean as soon as: 'once he left, we ate'
something over is finished

explanation.surface: A quick check carried out the moment the job is done.
explanation.definitionFit: A quick look over something, a cursory examination.

clue.text: Do astronauts go mad when they see this "Keep off" sign?

definitions.text: Do astronauts go mad when they see this "Keep off" sign?

parts.words: Do astronauts go mad when they see this "Keep off" sign?
parts.note: plays on a lunar body that is wholly occupied, like a 'no vacancies' notice, and the old belief that it drives people mad

explanation.surface: Wondering whether space travellers are driven crazy by a 'keep off' notice.
explanation.walkthrough: A moon that is 'full' cannot take visitors, so it is a 'Keep off' sign to astronauts; and lunacy was once blamed on the moon at its brightest phase.
explanation.definitionFit: The phase when the whole lunar disc is lit, long linked with madness, and 'full' like a house with no room.

clue.text: Actor's publicity spot ?

parts.note: reads as an advertising slot, but the spot is the circle of light thrown on a stage

explanation.surface: An actor's advertising slot.
explanation.walkthrough: Before electric light, stages were lit by burning quicklime; the phrase now means public attention, and a spot is literally a spotlight.
explanation.definitionFit: The old stage spotlight, and by extension the glare of public attention.

clue.text: Hard-wearing material for a trunk road.

definitions.meaning: a track made of tree trunks laid side by side across swampy ground

explanation.surface: A tough fabric suitable for a main road.
explanation.walkthrough: A 'trunk road' in Britain is a main road, but here it is a road of logs, called after the ribbed cloth it resembles.
explanation.definitionFit: A durable ribbed cotton fabric; a log road over a bog is named after its ridged look.

clue.text: Moor where boffins' work

parts.note: read as an instruction, the answer says take ROOM and turn it back, which spells this word

explanation.surface: A stretch of moorland where scientists do their research.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Boffins' is British slang for research scientists, who traditionally work out of sight in a back room.
explanation.definitionFit: A secluded office behind the scenes, where scientists and planners work away from the public.

clue.text: Veto his unhappy exile '

parts.note: to veto is to ban

indicators.note: unhappy here means disturbed, so the letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: Someone forbids his miserable banishment.
explanation.walkthrough: 'unhappy' signals an anagram of HIS, which follows BAN.
explanation.definitionFit: To send someone away from their country as a punishment.

clue.text: Physicist bilingually announces arrival of his first-born

parts.note: a new father says 'I am a father', here in English for the verb
and in French for the noun: père means father

explanation.surface: A scientist proudly tells everyone in two languages that his first child has been born.
explanation.walkthrough: 'bilingually' tells you the announcement mixes languages: English AM plus French PÈRE, 'I am father'. André-Marie Ampère was the French physicist who gave his name to the unit of current.
explanation.definitionFit: André-Marie Ampère was a French scientist who founded the study of electromagnetism.

clue.text: No trace' can be found, of this legislator

indicators.note: the letters can be found rearranged as another word, signalling an anagram

explanation.surface: A lawmaker of whom no sign remains.
explanation.walkthrough: 'can be found' signals an anagram of NO TRACE; 'of this' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: One who enacts laws, that is a lawmaker.

clue.text: Time to dine on mince

indicators.note: to mince is to chop up finely, so these words are cut up and reassembled

explanation.surface: It's time to have a meal of minced meat.
explanation.walkthrough: 'mince' looks like the meal, but it is the anagram signal on TO DINE ON.
explanation.definitionFit: Midday, an old poetic word for the hour of twelve.

clue.text: A trunk with tangled roots

indicators.note: tangled means twisted into disorder, so the letters are mixed up

explanation.surface: A tree trunk with knotted roots.
explanation.walkthrough: 'trunk' suggests a tree, which suits the roots, but means the human body without head or limbs.
explanation.definitionFit: The body's main part without head and limbs.

clue.text: Partially scalp a camel to 'get the wool

indicators.note: Partially says the answer is a run of letters hidden inside the words that follow

parts.note: the letters run across the end of one word into the next

explanation.surface: A grim instruction to shave part of a camel's head to get its fleece.
explanation.walkthrough: The draft's definition took in 'to get the', which are link words: the answer is the wool itself. The camel fits the surface, since this South American animal is a camel relative.
explanation.definitionFit: The fine fleece of a llama-like South American animal, woven into soft cloth.

clue.text: Confound it—-have a' go!

parts.note: a go is an attempt, a bash, as in 'have a bash'

explanation.surface: An exasperated person cursing and telling someone to give it a try.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Confound it' reads as an oath, but 'Confound' alone is the definition; 'it' and 'have' are links, with 'have a go' giving 'have a bash'.
explanation.definitionFit: To abash is to embarrass or disconcert someone.

clue.text: A life-time of bridge

definitions.meaning: to bridge, or the stretch a bridge covers

explanation.surface: A lifetime's devotion to the card game.
explanation.walkthrough: 'bridge' suggests the card game but is the structure crossing a gap.
explanation.definitionFit: A stretch of time such as a life; also the reach of an arch or the act of crossing a gap.

clue.text: Southern fruit for this side of the family

parts.note: S is the standard abbreviation for south or southern
a pear is a fruit

explanation.surface: Fruit from the south passed down one branch of the family.
explanation.walkthrough: The 'spear side' is an old term for the male line of descent, as opposed to the 'distaff side', the female line.
explanation.definitionFit: The male line of a family is called the spear side, from the weapon men carried.

clue.text: Parent goes mad with gun-disgusting !

indicators.note: something that goes mad runs wild, so these letters are thrown into a new order

explanation.surface: A parent going berserk with a firearm is appalling.
explanation.walkthrough: 'goes mad' signals an anagram of PARENT together with GUN; 'with' just joins them.
explanation.definitionFit: Repugnant means offensive or revolting, the same as something that disgusts.

clue.text: Cruncher for instance, not guilty of daylight robbery

definitions.meaning: Jerry Cruncher in Dickens's A Tale of Two Cities secretly digs up corpses for sale
a grave robber worked at night, so never robbed by day

explanation.surface: A man who chews loudly is cleared of an open theft.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cruncher' looks like a description, but it is Jerry Cruncher, the 'resurrection man' of Dickens's A Tale of Two Cities. 'Daylight robbery' is British slang for overcharging; these thieves robbed graves by night.
explanation.definitionFit: A resurrectionist who stole corpses from graves for medical schools, always working under cover of darkness.
